---
title: "Analysis 2: Which amino acids matter most for binding? Alanine screening"
author: "Luis Sebastian Galán, Laura Grenaa Jensen, Taniya Dey and Thota Kanishka Rao"
format: html
---

## Aim

Replacing an amino acid with alanine removes its side chain beyond the
beta-carbon. If binding gets much weaker (large positive ΔΔG), that amino acid
was probably important for the interface. Here we group single-point mutations
to alanine by their *starting* amino acid (e.g. all W -> A together) and compare the mean experimental ΔΔG.

A positive mean ΔΔG means binding generally got weaker when that amino acid was
replaced with alanine.

## The Setup

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| message: false
library("tidyverse")
library("here")
```
```{r}

#| label: settings
# Decisions made in this analysis (be ready to justify them):
min_n     <- 3   # groups smaller than this are flagged, not interpreted
ph_cutoff <- 7.4 # same rule as 04_describe: assay pH <= cutoff = "low", otherwise "high"
```

## Loading data

This document only needs `data/03_dat_aug.csv`, so it runs on its own.

```{r}
#| label: load
dat <- read_csv(
  file = here("data", "03_dat_aug.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

glimpse(dat)
```

### Column names

The names below were checked against `02_clean.qmd` and `03_augment.qmd`. Left side =
name used in this document, right side = name in your data.

```{r}
#| label: rename-columns
dat <- dat |>
  rename(
    complex   = pdb,             # complex identifier, confirmed from 02_clean
    from_aa   = mut_from,        # starting amino acid (one letter), confirmed from 03_augment
    to_aa     = mut_to,          # amino acid it was mutated to (one letter), confirmed from 03_augment
    ddg_exp   = ddg              # experimental ddG (kcal/mol), confirmed from 02_clean
    # assay_ph already has the right name in the data
  )
```

## Selecting single-point mutations to alanine

```{r}
#| label: filter-ala
ala_dat <- dat |>
  filter(
    str_length(from_aa) == 1,
    to_aa == "A",
    from_aa != "A",
    !is.na(ddg_exp),
    !is.na(complex),
    # 1DVF is an antibody-antibody complex that 02_clean includes twice (roles
    # swapped), so each of its measurements is in the data two times. Keep only
    # the copy where the mutated chain is renamed to H or L.
    !(complex == "1DVF" & !mut_chain %in% c("H", "L"))
  )

ala_dat |>
  summarise(
    n_mutations = n(),
    n_complexes = n_distinct(complex),
    n_start_aa  = n_distinct(from_aa)
  )
```

## Mean ΔΔG per starting amino acid

```{r}
#| label: ala-summary
ala_summary <- ala_dat |>
  group_by(from_aa) |>
  summarise(
    n_mut     = n(),
    n_complex = n_distinct(complex),
    mean_ddg  = mean(ddg_exp),
    median_ddg = median(ddg_exp),
    n_capped  = sum(ddg_exp >= 8),
    .groups   = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    small_group = n_mut < min_n,
    axis_label  = str_c(from_aa, "  (n = ", n_mut, ", ", n_complex, " complexes)")
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(mean_ddg))

ala_summary
```

```{r}
#| label: ala-dotplot
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6
ala_plot <- ala_summary |>
  mutate(
    axis_label  = fct_reorder(axis_label, mean_ddg),
    group_size  = if_else(small_group, str_c("n < ", min_n), str_c("n >= ", min_n))
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = mean_ddg, y = axis_label, size = n_mut, shape = group_size)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point() +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(16, 1)) +
  labs(
    title = "Mean experimental ddG when mutated to alanine",
    subtitle = "Positive = binding weaker. Hollow points: very few mutations, interpret with care",
    x = "Mean ddG (kcal/mol)",
    y = "Starting amino acid",
    size = "Mutations",
    shape = "Group size"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

ala_plot
```

```{r}
#| label: save-plot
ggsave(
  filename = here("results", "key_plot_ala_screen.png"),
  plot = ala_plot,
  width = 8,
  height = 6,
  dpi = 300
)
```

## Low vs High assay pH

First check how many measurements each starting amino acid has at low and high
pH. Only amino acids with at least `min_n` in both groups are compared.

```{r}
#| label: ph-counts
ala_ph <- ala_dat |>
  # Some values are ranges or pairs (e.g. 7.3_7.5). Like 04_describe, we use the
  # first number in each value.
  mutate(assay_ph = parse_number(as.character(assay_ph))) |>
  filter(!is.na(assay_ph)) |>
  mutate(ph_group = if_else(assay_ph <= ph_cutoff, "low", "high"))

ph_counts <- ala_ph |>
  count(from_aa, ph_group) |>
  complete(from_aa, ph_group, fill = list(n = 0)) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = ph_group, values_from = n) |>
  mutate(enough_both = low >= min_n & high >= min_n) |>
  arrange(desc(low + high))

ph_counts
```

```{r}
#| label: ph-plot
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6
enough_aa <- ph_counts |>
  filter(enough_both) |>
  pull(from_aa)

if (length(enough_aa) > 0) {
  ala_ph |>
    filter(from_aa %in% enough_aa) |>
    group_by(from_aa, ph_group) |>
    summarise(
      n_mut    = n(),
      mean_ddg = mean(ddg_exp),
      .groups  = "drop"
    ) |>
    mutate(from_aa = fct_reorder(from_aa, mean_ddg)) |>
    ggplot(aes(x = mean_ddg, y = from_aa, colour = ph_group, size = n_mut)) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.8) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c(low = "#0072B2", high = "#D55E00")) +
    labs(
      title = "Alanine screening split by assay pH",
      x = "Mean ddG (kcal/mol)",
      y = "Starting amino acid",
      colour = "Assay pH",
      size = "Mutations"
    ) +
    theme_minimal()
} else {
  message("No amino acid has enough data at both low and high pH, plot skipped.")
}
```

## Conclusion

We grouped 328 single-point mutations to alanine by the amino acid that was
replaced. All 19 starting amino acids have a positive mean ΔΔG, so on average
binding got weaker.

Cysteine (5.52) and methionine (2.78) have the highest means, but they rest on
only 1 and 4 mutations (1 and 2 complexes), so we do not interpret them. Among
groups with more data, tryptophan (2.52; 12 mutations, 6 complexes), histidine
(2.20; 14, 11) and tyrosine (1.86; 47, 11) have the largest means, followed by
phenylalanine (1.52; 16, 11). Tyrosine is the best supported. Serine (0.30),
threonine (0.49) and glutamine (0.64) have the smallest means among well-sampled groups.

## Comparison with the chemical-group analysis

`05_analysis_2.qmd` and '05_analysis_2.qmd' look at the same alanine mutations from different angles, and the two views complement each other.

**Our approach.** We keep every starting amino acid separate and describe it:
mean and median ΔΔG, the number of mutations and complexes behind each point,
and how many values are capped at 8 kcal/mol. The dot plot shows at a glance
which amino acids matter most and how much data supports each one. We also
split the data by assay pH, which shows which amino acids have enough
measurements to compare later.

**The chemical-group approach.** Grouping amino acids by chemistry gives larger
groups (for example 98 polar rows), so it can test differences with ANOVA and
pairwise comparisons, and it can adjust for mutation location and structure.
This adds something our descriptive view cannot: evidence that the differences
are not only due to which chain or complex a mutation happened to be in.

**Results.** Both analyses give the same picture: aromatic and positive amino
acids have the highest ΔΔG when replaced by alanine, and polar amino acids the
lowest. The chemical-group analysis finds that, after adjustment, aromatic
mutations were 0.95 kcal/mol and positive mutations 0.78 kcal/mol higher than
polar ones. Our per-amino-acid view shows what sits inside those groups. Within
the aromatic group tryptophan (2.52) is highest, followed by tyrosine (1.86) and phenylalanine (1.52). Within the positive group histidine (2.20) is higher than arginine (1.34) and lysine (1.07). These differences would be hidden in a group mean.

**Together.** The amino acid view shows which residues drive the pattern, and
the chemical-group models show that the pattern holds after accounting for
chain and structure.
